title: Regarding AI game development, I think I just need to vent.
author: Effective-Sweet2606
selftext:
So, I'm a person who's been completely blind since birth and I'm trying to develop a game aimed at other totally blind people. It's quite a large project, I admit, a completely audio-only savanna simulator with screen reader integration, where you control a wild animal, that is, without any images.

I'm using Python and the gpt chat (maybe I should change it, just use claude) only in the free templates, because I can't afford to pay for something like that, but honestly, I started to get disappointed when the AI ​​started to get lost, to guide me on things I didn't even want to program at the moment and to forget things we had already defined, even when I opened a new chat within the project. It also seems to find pending issues and gaps even where there aren't any, or where there shouldn't be. And I don't know if it's normal or if the AI ​​is just stalling to keep the conversation going.

And I can't even understand the technical terms. I've never been good at math, this is my first time dealing with programming, but I thought I could learn with AI. I mean, I make mods for games using AI, so it shouldn't be that difficult...

But I'm not managing.

I'm feeling really bad, because while some people can develop games in a month, I've been just running on [main.py](http://main.py) and script core for days. I have a bunch of empty folders that I don't even know when or how I'm going to fill them. I feel like everything is just a mess, and I don't know if that's normal or if I did something wrong. And I just wanted this to work out, because it's something I want to make available to other people in the future, since playing this kind of thing has always been my dream, but I never could because of my blindness and lack of financial resources.



In short, I don't know if I'm just being impatient, if I'm just using the wrong prompt (maybe I should have directly asked them to develop a functional zip file), or if I'm just overthinking it... I just know that I already feel like a failure, and I'll feel like total garbage if I end up giving up.

comments.author: Any-Ad-1892
comments.body:

comments.author: Electronic-Movie4208
comments.body:
Hey, please don't give up on this project! I'm also developing a game with AI assistant, and trust me, I've experienced the same frustrations with AI forgetting things, changing plans, and creating problems that weren't there.

One thing that's helped me is keeping a project document that explains exactly what we're building, what's already completed, and what needs to happen next. That way, when the AI loses track, you can give it that document instead of starting over.

I'd also suggest building one small, playable feature at a time instead of trying to tackle the entire game. And don't compare your progress to people claiming they built games in a month. You're creating something unique, and accessibility adds another layer of complexity.

I'd genuinely love to see your project succeed. If you ever want to exchange ideas or discuss development challenges, feel free to reach out!

comments.author: Honest_Accident_8348
comments.body:
1) agree - change to Claude asap! 
2) why python?  Is there a particular reason you chose python for your game?  I made some python games early on because I can code python - but found JavaScript much easier to work with, and much better results. JS will also allow you to host it online without having to run a py file on a costly server.  
3) ask Claude to make a markup file to record every decision and read the markup file before each session.   That may help with the confusion, as it will prevent ai from overwriting a previous decision.  

Making an inclusive game is awesome and noble effort for people underrepresented in gaming.  You shouldn’t give up, and definitly don’t feel like a failure.  I had multiple games i considered failures before I made one I really liked - but each was a learning opportunity

comments.author: drahgon
comments.body:
I would work on one feature at a time AI can get not lost, but can get way too creative and go on its own direction if you try to do too much at once. it’s own patterns that it made in the code, it starts to take those as fact when you in reality want to change core concepts, but it feels restricted by the restrictions it itself put it in place. A good idea is just start really slow. Get one feature going and then add and just really direct it instead of giving it a lot of creative freedom.

I would start from scratch at this point

comments.author: DCON-creates
comments.body:
It's just because you're learning. ChatGPT is not great for game dev in continuation- it's fine for isolated features but it'll send you in loops otherwise (which is presumably what's happening now). Claude code would likely nail down what you're trying to do pretty well.

Programming is still incredibly difficult, even with AI assistance, you may see some people here saying "oh I one-shotted a game in a single prompt" or whatever, but ignore them, they really don't know what they're doing and are setting a standard that shouldn't even exist (if they're not lying, which most of them are)

Anyway, this frustration you're feeling is called learning ;) just keep practicing, you'll get there eventually.

comments.author: FordEngineerman
comments.body:
Something I quickly learned when starting to learn game dev is that the AI cannot handle single large programs. It gets lost and forgets things. The program needs architecture work where it is broken into components the AI can manageably read into its limited context. And the AI needs to be able to make memory files for itself with various rules and practices for the specific project - otherwise it will forget between sessions.

Working purely in a chat window is very very difficult for that reason. Giving it a full folder/github to work in that it has access to allows it to automatically make and read the memories it needs whenever it needs and essentially offload excess context to files it makes.

comments.author: je386
comments.body:
First of all, don't expect game development to be fast at all. I am a professional software developer for business software and on my second game since 13 month now, while heavily using AI.

Second: use a coding agent like claude or github copilot coding agent, whichever is affordable.

When you use a coding agent, you can save general rules in a agents.md (or copilot-instructions.md or claude.md, depending on what you use). That means that the basic general rules are read every time rhe agent runs and you don't have to repeat yourself.

comments.author: HECRETSECRET
comments.body:
First flip to claude. 100 percent. Get the smartest model you can on claude. The 20 dollar plan caa do. Gemini and Chatgpt can program but Claude is the best of laying it all out for you and taking care of all the small things and actually getting things done AND Programming. It can do a prototype within an hour something you want and its actually good.  

1. Lay out everything you want your game to be in a text document. The first chat will be claude on its smartest model, like fable to design this game and to give a prompt to project.
 
2. Use shared space like drive for all the files and notes or Claude can use github. Follow claudes reccomendations. Glaude will just set up a github repo for you or guide you through it. 

3. After the plan is laid out you can switch to Opus for building. The smartest models are there for planning and archtecture. Then its a daily drive of building it out. 
 

Keep in mind: if you dont know ask a smart ai what would a prompt be for you want you want. Claude hands and above is the best at reasoning and showing things in a gentle way how you actually want them.

comments.author: RygaLikeTyga

comments.author: OneManGameStudio76
comments.body:
The frustration is normal. AI agents lose context because they don't share memory between chats, not because you are doing something wrong.

I run multiple coding agents on the same project. They overwrite each other's work if you let them. I had to build a local service to govern which agent can touch which file and enforce workspace authorization. Without that, the code becomes a mess of conflicting changes within hours.

The "pending issues" you are seeing are likely hallucinations. Models invent problems to keep generating text. If a test doesn't fail, the feature works. Don't trust the summary; trust the output.

Start small. One system at a time. Get one mechanic working before adding another layer.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
you fall into a typical trap by listening to reddit too much

reddit loves pushing people to do ai-assist dev but it is actually silly if you aren't technical to begin with. Even for technical people like myself, ai-assist hasn't been necessary since 2026... people just keep pushing it because they want some identity/pride with what they do...

forget about anything technical about your game.

break down your game into goals, constraints, checkpoints. that's it.

Let AI drive and you will get a workable game eventually. AIs in 2026 are absurdly strong.

also, you are just making a game. As long as it runs correctly for a long enough period of time i.e. 6 hours without crashing... you are good.

so yeah, just let AI drive and you have your game. That's it.

TLDR; you are actually holding back AI if you insist on participating with the technical aspect without being technical enough. you make AI's "life" easier if you just let it do the heavy lifting without carrying you technically

comments.author: LiteratureSelect4478
comments.body:
Chatgpt does that,  design a plan for the entire program.  Then design plans for each step.  Each step has a plan and steps.  If you do each step and stick to the plan ai can't get side tracked 

Just tell it to log every step along the way and anything else or extra to add at the end - read not code it but note it down as that's a plan to fix rhe game when your done basically  

Then audit the entire game and ask it to refactor it - plan and execute cos then ai your using understand your program better.

Stops the exact problem your dealing with.   


But good luck

comments.author: No_Climate_3286
comments.body:
The frustration is real man, what I did when I started was to give it premise and tell it to keep asking me questions to extract information on what I want functionally and whenever it threw a jargon I asked it to explain it.

By the end of it we had a detailed plan broken into steps which I took to a coding agent.

comments.author: fourtenight
comments.body:
OP, I hope this doesn't get buried but I think you should open source the project under strict contribution guidelines and have some of us help you make progress. I run the 100 a month Claude plan for my own stuff and would love to contribute to something like this. 

The truth is that under the free plans you usually only have access to models like Luna and Haiku/Sonnet which can write code but require extremely strict scope/specs so any thing you build with it would fall apart pretty quick if you don't know what you're doing.
